17409.title: C# Numeric Types
17409.heading: C# Numeric Types
17409.content:
C# provides signed and unsigned integer types with different bit widths, along with floating-point and decimal types for non-whole values. A type's range and precision determine which values it can represent and how much storage it uses.

`double` is efficient for scientific and general real-number computation but represents many decimal fractions approximately. `decimal` stores base-10 values with higher decimal precision and is often better for money. Numeric suffixes and explicit types prevent a literal from being interpreted with an unintended default type.

17412.content:
Method overloading defines several members with the same name but different parameter signatures. The compiler selects an overload from the number, types, order, and passing modes of the arguments supplied at the call site.

Overloads present one conceptual operation across several input forms. They should preserve related meaning; unrelated behavior hidden under one name makes selection harder to understand. Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads because it is not part of the call's argument signature.

A C# project selects a language version through its compiler and project configuration. The target framework normally supplies a compatible default, while a `LangVersion` setting can request a specific installed version, the latest major version, the latest available version, or a preview.

Language and runtime versions are related but not identical. C# 8.0 features require a compiler that understands them, and some features also depend on framework types or runtime behavior. Pinning a version makes the project's syntax expectations explicit instead of inheriting whatever a future toolchain happens to choose.

17418.heading: C# Iteration Statements
17418.content:
C# provides `while`, `do`, `for`, and `foreach` statements for repetition. A `while` loop tests before each iteration, a `do` loop runs once before testing, and a `for` loop gathers initialization, condition, and update into one header.

`foreach` obtains an enumerator and repeatedly advances it through a sequence's current items. The iteration variable is not a mechanism for replacing the underlying current item. Choosing a loop should make the stopping condition and source of progress easy to verify.

Common .NET interfaces support comparison, enumeration, formatting, serialization, and deterministic disposal. Implementation can be public or explicit; explicit members are reached through the interface view and help separate overlapping contracts from the class's ordinary surface.

Braces make the controlled block unambiguous even when it contains one statement. Omitting them can turn a later edit into a logic error because indentation does not determine C# control flow. C# grammar defines how tokens combine into legal statements, blocks, expressions, declarations, and comments. Vocabulary consists of the keywords, type names, member names, and identifiers used within that structure.

Methods behave like verbs because they perform actions, while types, fields, and variables act like nouns because they name kinds of things and stored values. The compiler enforces grammar, but clear naming and consistent formatting make the same valid program easier for people to understand.

Parameters define the typed inputs a C# function accepts, while arguments are the values supplied at a call site. A parameter can receive a value normally, copy data out through `out`, accept input by reference with `ref`, or receive a read-only reference through `in`.

Passing mode affects whether assignments inside the function can change the caller's variable. Clear names and narrow types communicate the contract, and validation near the function boundary prevents an invalid argument from producing a failure far from its source.

17433.title: C# Fields and Access Modifiers
17433.heading: C# Fields and Access Modifiers
17433.content:
A field stores data inside a C# type or object. Instance fields belong to each object, while static fields belong to the type as a whole. A field can use any type, including arrays and collections.

Access modifiers control where a member is visible. Public exposes it broadly, private confines it to the declaring type, and protected or internal forms expose it to inheritance or an assembly boundary. Encapsulation chooses the narrowest visibility that still supports the intended collaboration.

17436.heading: C# Extension Methods
17436.content:
An extension method is a static method that can be called with instance-style syntax on another type. Its first parameter uses `this` to identify the extended type, and importing the declaring namespace makes the method available to callers.

Extension methods add reusable operations when a type cannot or should not be inherited, including sealed framework types such as strings. They do not modify the original type or gain access to its private state; they remain ordinary static functions with convenient call syntax.

The event boundary restricts outside code to subscription and unsubscription rather than arbitrary invocation. Event arguments carry details about the occurrence, and a custom event-argument type can add domain-specific data beyond the conventional sender reference.

An enum marked for flags assigns powers of two so several values can be combined in one bit field. Bitwise operations and `HasFlag` can then add, remove, or test individual choices without treating their combination as an unrelated number.

17445.heading: C# Delegates
17445.content:
A C# delegate is a type-safe reference to a method with a specified parameter and return signature. Code can store the delegate, pass it as data, and invoke the referenced method later without depending directly on its declaring type.

Several compatible method references can be combined into a multicast delegate and invoked in sequence. Delegates form the basis of events and also appear as the function arguments used by LINQ operators and other callback-oriented APIs.

17448.heading: C# Constructors
17448.content:
A constructor runs when a C# object is created and establishes its valid initial state. It has the type's name, has no return type, and can accept parameters that supply values required by the new instance.

Several constructors can be overloaded for different initialization paths, and one can delegate to another to centralize shared work. Construction is a useful invariant boundary: an object should not leave it missing values that every later method assumes exist.

17457.heading: C# Checked Arithmetic
17457.content:
Integer arithmetic can exceed a type's representable range and wrap to another value. A `checked` context converts that silent overflow into an exception, while `unchecked` explicitly permits the wraparound behavior.

The correct policy depends on the operation. Silent wrapping may be intentional in low-level algorithms, but business quantities and conversions usually need a detectable failure. Compiler settings can establish a default, and local checked or unchecked blocks can state exceptions to that policy.

The `Convert` class supplies conversions whose behavior can differ from a direct cast, particularly around rounding and supported representations. Conversion is not merely a syntax problem: the program must decide what loss, rounding, overflow, or invalid input means in its domain.

C# does not treat arbitrary integers or objects as implicit truth values. Requiring a Boolean condition keeps control flow explicit: a program must state the comparison or predicate that decides whether a branch or loop continues.

17466.title: C# Bitwise and Shift Operators
17466.heading: C# Bitwise and Shift Operators
17466.content:
Bitwise operators combine integer operands one binary position at a time. AND preserves positions set in both operands, OR preserves positions set in either, XOR preserves positions that differ, and complement reverses the bits.

Shift operators move a value's bit pattern left or right. These operations support compact flags, masks, and low-level numeric transformations. Unlike conditional logical operators, the nonconditional Boolean forms evaluate both operands, which matters when those expressions have side effects.

17469.title: C# Async and Await
17469.heading: C# Async and Await
17469.content:
An `async` method can use `await` to pause its logical execution until an awaitable operation completes. The method returns control to its caller instead of blocking the current thread and later resumes from the suspended point.

Asynchronous code improves responsiveness and scalability for waiting-heavy operations, but it does not make CPU work inherently faster. Tasks should normally be awaited, exceptions must be observed, and cancellation should be propagated through the operation graph.

The conference-counter example uses waiting customers to motivate nonblocking work. In an application, `await` yields while an asynchronous operation is incomplete instead of occupying a thread solely to wait; many requests can therefore make progress with fewer blocked workers.

17472.title: C# Assignment and Logical Operators
17472.heading: C# Assignment and Logical Operators
17472.content:
Assignment operators store a result in a variable. Compound forms combine an operation with assignment, while null-coalescing assignment stores a fallback only when the current value is null.

Logical operators combine or invert Boolean expressions. Conditional `&&` and `||` stop as soon as the result is known, so the right operand may not execute. This short-circuit behavior supports guarded access, such as checking that a reference is non-null before evaluating one of its members.

17475.content:
A Blender operator can toggle a viewport draw handler in response to a panel button. When the overlay is inactive, execution adds the handler and stores its reference; when active, execution removes it and clears the reference. A window-level Boolean can keep the panel's displayed state consistent with the actual handler.

This lifecycle solves a problem with one-off scripts: a persistent draw callback may otherwise remain attached until Blender restarts. The button gives the user control, while unregistration provides a final cleanup path if the add-on is disabled during drawing.

A button state transition is a change between released and pressed states across input updates. Just pressed occurs when the previous state was off and the current state is on; just released is the inverse transition.

Transitions let a game trigger one event per activation while still supporting held-state behavior for continuous actions. They require retaining at least the previous sampled state of the control.

17481.heading: Business-Linked Pricing
17481.content:
Business-linked pricing ties a cloud-service charge to a business performance indicator rather than a purely technical service metric. The intent is to reflect the service's contribution to the organization's business model.

Its main difficulty is attribution: a business result usually depends on several people, processes, and external conditions. The parties therefore need a defensible relationship between the chosen indicator and the service before using it as a payment basis.

17484.title: Business Translator
17484.heading: Business Translator
17484.content:
A business translator combines data literacy with industry and functional expertise so analytical findings can be incorporated into everyday processes. The role connects technical teams with the people responsible for operational choices.

Translation includes framing a useful question, interpreting model output, and explaining what action the evidence supports. It addresses an organizational barrier that better algorithms alone cannot solve.

17487.heading: Business Process Reengineering
17487.content:
Business process reengineering redesigns work at the process level instead of automating every existing step unchanged. It identifies necessary processes and workflows, removes or changes those that do not contribute, and implements a more efficient future arrangement.

A cloud transition creates an opportunity for this redesign because applications, information services, and complete business-process services can replace different portions of the old flow. The technology choice should follow the redesigned process rather than define it prematurely.

17490.heading: Business Process Management
17490.content:
Business process management is the collection of methods, tools, and technologies used to design, enact, analyze, optimize, and control business processes. It treats recurring work as an explicit flow that can be measured and improved.

Cloud business-process services depend on this discipline because automation is valuable only after the process, participants, information, and desired outcome are understood. A workflow may contain both automated and human stages.

17493.heading: Business Process Interface
17493.content:
A business process interface defines how one process interacts with another. It identifies the information shared, the event or control signal that starts the exchange, the expected result, and any timing or service conditions.

Most processes are not independent. A payroll process, for example, needs changes from human resources and approved overtime from management, so its interfaces must be specified before the process can be outsourced or automated safely.

17496.heading: Business Process Information Interface
17496.content:
A business process information interface defines the data one process supplies to or receives from another. It specifies the meaning, structure, currency, and ownership of information needed for the receiving process to act correctly.

The interface complements a [[Business Process Control Interface]], which triggers the action. Separating control from information clarifies whether a message means that work should begin or merely provides facts that may be used later.

17505.title: Business Intelligence versus Prediction
17505.heading: Business Intelligence versus Prediction
17505.content:
Business intelligence integrates and summarizes data for reports and decision support, often using a warehouse and multidimensional queries. Prediction instead trains a model from historic examples to estimate an unknown target for new instances. A report describing past sales is not by itself a forecast of future customer behavior.

The two activities can reinforce each other. A warehouse may supply cleaned historical data and shorten model preparation, while scored predictions can return to dashboards or applications. Their distinct goals still require different evaluation: a correct aggregation and a model that generalizes to unseen cases are not the same accomplishment.

Automation does not remove the need for domain understanding. The analytical system must connect its objective, input data, learning method, and evaluation to the business decision it is supposed to improve.

17511.heading: Business Continuity Plan
17511.content:
A business continuity plan defines how essential operations will continue through a disaster, emergency, attack, provider outage, or other major disruption. It connects service priorities with alternate people, processes, locations, systems, and communication paths.

For a critical cloud service, the plan should address loss of the provider as well as failure inside the consumer's own application. Tested interoperability with secondary services is necessary if work or data must move across provider boundaries.

17514.title: Burndown Chart
17514.heading: Burndown Chart
17514.content:
A burndown chart plots estimated work remaining against time in a fixed interval. Its trend helps a team see whether its present rate is likely to reach the end of a Sprint or release with the intended scope completed.

The chart is a forecast and conversation trigger, not an individual performance measure. Since the end date is fixed, the team can adapt scope or approach when the trend exposes a mismatch.

17517.title: Bundle Adjustment
17517.heading: Bundle Adjustment
17517.content:
Bundle adjustment jointly refines camera poses and three-dimensional feature positions by minimizing reprojection error across many observations. Rather than improving each frame independently, it uses the shared geometry connecting landmarks and views.

The optimization can correct accumulated inconsistencies in a visual map, especially after loop closure supplies a long-range constraint. Its computational cost means a real-time system may apply it selectively or in a parallel mapping process.

17519.sourceSearchName: buoyancy driven thermal flow buoyancy driven thermal flow

17520.sourceSearchName: buoyancy driven thermal flow buoyancy driven thermal flow
17520.title: Buoyancy-Driven Thermal Flow
17520.heading: Buoyancy-Driven Thermal Flow
17520.content:
Heating changes fluid density, and gravity then produces a body force that can drive circulation. Warmer, less dense fluid rises while cooler, denser fluid descends, transporting energy in addition to molecular conduction.

This natural-convection feedback appears in a cup or kettle even without an imposed inlet velocity. A coupled model needs gravity, a consistent density law, and suitable walls or free surfaces to resolve the circulation rather than replacing it with a fixed [[Convective Heat Transfer Coefficient|boundary coefficient]].

A bus network topology connects every node through one shared communication channel. A transmission placed on the bus can reach the attached nodes, which must determine whether the message is intended for them.

The shared channel limits infrastructure, but it also concentrates contention and failure. If the central bus becomes unavailable, every attached node can become isolated at once.

17529.heading: Bulletin Board System
17529.content:
A bulletin board system was a computer that callers reached by modem to exchange messages and files. Many were operated locally by individuals or small groups and could run on an ordinary personal computer with storage.

Long-distance costs encouraged boards to forward material to one another during cheaper hours. Their communities anticipated later forums and social networks.

17532.title: Builder Pattern
17532.heading: Builder Pattern
17532.content: The builder pattern separates the construction process for a complex object from the finished object's representation. A builder can collect or sequence required parts, validate that construction is complete, and then produce the object. This is useful when a constructor with many optional arguments obscures which combinations are valid, but it adds little when an object can be created clearly in one step.

17535.title: Build Pipeline
17535.heading: Build Pipeline
17535.content:
A build pipeline is the automated sequence that turns a source revision into verified deployment artifacts. It restores dependencies, compiles the React and ASP.NET Core applications, runs selected tests, and publishes the outputs needed by the release process.

Every result belongs to a particular source version. A failed required step stops that version from being treated as a releasable artifact.

17538.title: Build Iteration
17538.heading: Build Iteration
17538.content:
Build iteration is the loop from committing a change through building, automated testing, and sharing a verified result. Frequent small commits reduce the amount of unintegrated work and make failures easier to isolate.

A reliable [[Continuous Integration]] system shortens this loop by building each supported configuration and reporting defects quickly enough for the responsible developer to respond.

17541.title: Build Agent
17541.heading: Build Agent
17541.content:
A build agent is the execution environment that runs the steps in a build pipeline. It checks out the source, invokes the required toolchains, executes tests, and places generated files where the pipeline can publish them.

The agent's installed tools and operating environment affect whether a build is reproducible. Pipeline steps should declare the needed runtime behavior rather than depend on accidental machine state.

17544.title: Build Artifact
17544.heading: Build Artifact
17544.content:
A build artifact is a versioned output produced by a successful build pipeline for later deployment. It contains the publishable application files rather than requiring the release pipeline to rebuild from an unverified working tree.

The artifact connects one tested source revision to every environment that receives it. Preserving that identity prevents staging and production from accidentally running packages built from different code.

17547.title: Buchsbaum-Eisenbud Exactness Criterion
17547.heading: Buchsbaum-Eisenbud Exactness Criterion
17547.content:
The Buchsbaum-Eisenbud criterion tests exactness of a finite complex of finitely generated free modules using ranks of consecutive maps and depths of their determinantal ideals.

At each position, adjacent ranks must add to the rank of the middle free module, and the ideal of the expected minors must contain a regular sequence of sufficient length. These conditions convert exactness into computable algebraic data.

17550.sourceSearchName: buchberger s algorithm buchberger s algorithm
17550.title: Buchberger's Algorithm
17550.heading: Buchberger's Algorithm
17550.content:
Buchberger's algorithm constructs a [[Gröbner Basis]] from generators of a polynomial ideal. It forms [[S-Polynomial]]s for pairs of basis elements, reduces them by the current basis, and adds every nonzero remainder.

The process stops when all relevant S-polynomials reduce to zero. At that point the basis has compatible leading reductions and supports ideal membership and elimination computations.

17556.title: Brooks's Law
17556.heading: Brooks's Law
17556.content:
Brooks's Law states that adding people to a late software project can make it later. New members require onboarding, create additional communication paths, and consume the attention of experienced people before they contribute effectively.

The effect is strongest when work is highly interdependent and cannot be partitioned cleanly. Addressing constraints, scope, and coordination may improve delivery more than increasing headcount.

17559.title: Broadcast Message
17559.heading: Broadcast Message
17559.content:
A broadcast message is a real-time event sent to multiple connected clients. Server code uses the hub context to name the event and provide a payload, and every intended recipient with a matching handler can react to it.

Broadcasting is appropriate when a change should be visible broadly, such as a newly added answer. More selective delivery is needed when data or authorization differs among recipients.

In message-oriented integration, a broadcast message is published under a topic so interested receivers can obtain it without the sender addressing each one individually. This contrasts with [[Point-to-Point Messaging]] and requires consistent topic and access rules.

17561.heading: Document

17562.sourceSearchName: broad network access broad network access
17562.title: Broad Network Access
17562.heading: Broad Network Access
17562.content:
Broad network access is the cloud characteristic that makes a service reachable through a network from different locations and suitable client devices. It separates access to a service from physical presence at the infrastructure that runs it.

The breadth of access depends on the deployment boundary. A [[Public Cloud]] is normally reached over the Internet, while a [[Private Cloud]] may restrict access to a private network. Increasing reach also increases the importance of authentication, secure channels, and endpoint protection.

17565.sourceSearchName: bring your own device bring your own device
17565.title: Bring Your Own Device
17565.heading: Bring Your Own Device
17565.content:
Bring your own device is an operating model in which people use personally chosen computers or mobile devices to reach organizational applications and information. The organization must support device diversity rather than managing one homogeneous hardware and software image.

Cloud applications make this model practical by moving shared services away from the individual device. Protected local storage, identity controls, endpoint security, remote data access, and clear user responsibility are necessary because the organization does not fully control the client.

17568.title: Breakpoint
17568.heading: Breakpoint
17568.content:
A breakpoint marks a source location where a [[Debugger]] should pause program execution. While paused, a developer can inspect variables, evaluate expressions, review the call stack, and step through subsequent operations.

A breakpoint inside a controller can expose server request state, while one in an Angular component can expose form or subscription state. Conditions can narrow the pause to a relevant case.
links: C Sharp Functions Diagnostics and Testing

17569.title: Breakpoint
17569.heading: References
links: C Sharp Functions Diagnostics and Testing

17571.title: Breakpoint Action
17571.heading: Breakpoint Action
17571.content:
A breakpoint action performs diagnostic work when execution reaches a breakpoint, such as writing a message to the output window. It can capture values without requiring the program to remain paused.

Actions can be combined with conditions so output is produced only for relevant states. This turns a breakpoint into a targeted trace point while retaining the option to stop execution when needed.

17573.sourceSearchName: breadth first search breadth first search
17573.title: Breadth-First Search
17573.heading: Document

17574.sourceSearchName: breadth first search breadth first search
17574.title: Breadth-First Search
17574.heading: Breadth-First Search
17574.content:
Breadth-first search explores a graph in layers of increasing edge count from the start node. A queue holds discovered nodes, and each node records whether it has been visited and which predecessor first reached it.

On an unweighted graph, the first discovered path to a node uses the fewest edges, so the algorithm guarantees a shortest path when one exists. Weighted travel costs require a method such as [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]] or [[A Star Search]].

17575.sourceSearchName: breadth first search breadth first search
17575.title: Breadth-First Search
17575.heading: References

17577.title: Branching Story
17577.heading: Branching Story
17577.content:
A branching story lets player choices select among multiple authored paths. Each branch may change events, available choices, or endings, allowing players to pursue different versions of the narrative.

Branches remain constrained by material the creators prepared. Wide divergence can require a large amount of content and make it difficult for every path to feel complete, so many designs use [[Reconverging Branches]] or concentrate variation near the ending.

17580.title: Braking Engine
17580.heading: Braking Engine
17580.content:
A braking engine is a predominantly [[Balancing Loop|balancing]] structure that drains a resource or reduces its future rate of gain. It creates friction that regulates progress and counteracts a reinforcing engine.

Brakes can preserve competition and pacing, but excessive friction leaves the player unable to act and can stop the game. They are therefore usually subsidiary loops within a [[Boosting Engine]], economy, or progression system.

17583.title: bpy.ops Operators
17583.heading: bpy.ops Operators
17583.content:
`bpy.ops` contains operator functions that commonly mirror actions available through Blender's interface. Object operators handle whole objects and general object utilities, mesh operators work with vertices, edges, and faces, and transform operators apply translation, rotation, or scaling.

Operators are imperative and context-sensitive: they act on the current selection, active object, and mode. This makes them concise for reproducing an interface workflow, but it also means a script must establish the expected context before invoking them. Direct access through [[bpy.data Datablocks]] is preferable when a specific named value should be read or assigned without depending on selection.

17585.title: bpy.context State
17585.heading: Document
17585.content:
2026-09-08 09:04

Tags: [[Blender Python Data and Operations]]

17586.title: bpy.context State
17586.heading: bpy.context State
17586.content:
`bpy.context` exposes the state in which a Blender operation is evaluated. It can identify the scene, mode, selected objects, active object, and data associated with the current interface area. Operator behavior often changes or becomes unavailable when this state does not meet its requirements.

Context is a convenient path to what the user is currently working with, but it is not a permanent identity for that data. When a script needs a particular object regardless of interface focus, [[Blender Object Lookup by Name]] through `bpy.data` makes that dependency explicit.

17588.title: bpy.data Datablocks

2026-09-08 09:04

Tags: [[Blender Python Data and Operations]]

17589.title: bpy.data Datablocks
17589.heading: bpy.data Datablocks
17589.content:
`bpy.data` exposes Blender's internal datablocks, including objects, meshes, materials, textures, images, and scenes. Datablocks separate an object's identity and placement from the underlying data that defines its geometry or appearance.

Direct datablock access is declarative: assigning a named object's location overwrites that property rather than applying a relative transformation to whatever happens to be selected. It is also a stable way to retrieve data by name, inspect nested relationships, create new data containers, or remove unused ones.

17591.title: bpy.app Module
17591.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Blender Python Data and Operations]]

17592.title: bpy.app Module
17592.heading: bpy.app Module
17592.content:
`bpy.app` exposes information and services belonging to the running Blender application rather than to a single scene object. Of particular importance, `bpy.app.handlers` stores lists of functions that Blender calls around events such as frame changes, rendering, loading, and saving.

Application handlers make scripts reactive instead of purely sequential. A function can update data before a scene refresh or run diagnostics after a file loads. Because these hooks outlive the immediate statement that installed them, their creation, removal, and persistence need deliberate lifecycle management.

17595.title: Box Plot
17595.heading: Box Plot
17595.content:
A box plot summarizes a continuous distribution through its median, quartiles, spread, and observations beyond the whiskers. It provides a compact view of center and asymmetry without requiring a choice of histogram bins.

Side-by-side box plots are especially useful for comparing the same outcome across groups. Their compactness can hide multimodality and sample-size differences, so they work best alongside numerical summaries and other distribution plots.

The source defines the box through the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles and places whiskers relative to the interquartile range. This design makes the display useful when a skewed distribution causes the mean and standard deviation to give an incomplete summary.

The book places box plots beside [[Violin Plot|violin plots]] for grouped continuous data. The compact quartile summary and the smoothed distribution view answer complementary questions about center, spread, skewness, and multiple modes.

17598.title: Bounding Sphere
17598.heading: Bounding Sphere
17598.content:
A bounding sphere encloses an object with a center point and radius. Two spheres intersect when the distance between their centers is no greater than the sum of their radii.

Comparing squared distance avoids an unnecessary square root. Spheres are cheap to test and unaffected by rotation, but they fit elongated or irregular models poorly and can report collisions where visible geometry remains separated.

17601.title: Bounded Interval
17601.heading: Bounded Interval
17601.content:
A bounded interval lies between two finite endpoints. Examples include

$$-1\leq x\leq2$$

and

$$-1<x<2.$$

Its length is the upper endpoint minus the lower endpoint, regardless of whether either boundary is included. Although the length is finite, the interval contains infinitely many [[Real Number]]s. Endpoint symbols determine membership: brackets or filled points include a boundary, while parentheses or open points exclude it.

17603.title: Bounded Context

17604.title: Bounded Context
17604.heading: Bounded Context
17604.content: A bounded context is the explicit boundary within which one [[Domain Model]] and [[Ubiquitous Language]] are internally consistent. The same word can represent different concepts in other contexts without forcing one object to contain every possible meaning. Inside the boundary, code, tests, data, and conversation share the model; across it, relationships and translations must be deliberate. Clear [[Bounded Context Ownership]] gives a team autonomy to change the model without continuous coordination over its internals.

17606.heading: Document

17607.sourceSearchName: bounded context ownership bounded context ownership
17607.title: Bounded Context Ownership
17607.heading: Bounded Context Ownership
17607.content: Bounded context ownership assigns responsibility for one [[Bounded Context]] to no more than one cross-functional team. One team may own several contexts, but splitting one context among several teams recreates continuous coordination over its language and internal model. Ownership includes the code, data, rules, and operational decisions inside the boundary. It turns [[Conway's Law]] into a design consideration: the organizational communication structure should reinforce, rather than undermine, the intended system boundaries.

17610.title: Bounded Complex
17610.heading: Bounded Complex
17610.content:
A complex is bounded below when all sufficiently low-degree terms are zero and bounded above when all sufficiently high-degree terms are zero. It is bounded when both conditions hold.

Boundedness limits the number of active homological positions. Finite projective and injective resolutions are bounded complexes whose lengths define projective or injective dimension.

17616.heading: Boundary in a Chain Complex
17616.content:
An n-boundary is an element in the image of the differential dₙ₊₁: Cₙ₊₁ → Cₙ. It is produced by applying the preceding map in a [[Chain Complex]].

Since dₙdₙ₊₁ = 0, every boundary lies in the kernel of dₙ and is therefore a [[Cycle in a Chain Complex]]. Homology identifies cycles that differ by a boundary.

17619.heading: Bottom-Up Network Communities
17619.content:
Bottom-up network communities emerged from hobbyists and ordinary users connecting bulletin boards, forums, and commercial services outside government research networks. Their priorities included conversation, identity, entertainment, and informal exchange.

The modern networked world formed when these social systems collided with top-down academic and military infrastructure. Protocols supplied interconnection, while communities supplied much of the demand and culture.

17622.title: Bottleneck
17622.heading: Bottleneck
17622.content:
A bottleneck is the constraint that most limits a system's throughput. Work accumulates before it while downstream capacity may be starved, making it visible through queues and rising cycle time.

Improvement focuses on one dominant constraint at a time: protect it from avoidable interruption, help it complete valuable work, and prevent excess upstream production. Once relieved, another constraint becomes limiting.

17625.title: Botometer
17625.heading: Botometer
17625.content:
Botometer is a social-bot detection system that computes a large collection of account, network, content, sentiment, and temporal features and returns automation-related scores. Its public interface makes a research classifier available for account assessment.

The system illustrates how feature breadth supports holistic detection. A score is model-dependent evidence rather than proof, and performance can change as platform behavior and bot strategies evolve.

17628.heading: Bot Conversation Turn
17628.content:
A bot conversation turn is one cycle in which an incoming activity is processed and zero or more outgoing activities are produced. The turn context provides the current message and the operation used to send the bot's response.

Conversation quality depends on more than one isolated turn because earlier answers can determine which information is missing next. The book's simplified bot chooses a response from the recognized current intent rather than implementing a deeper dialog state model.

17631.title: Botnet
17631.heading: Botnet
17631.content:
A botnet is a collection of compromised devices controlled together by an attacker. Each [[Zombie Computer]] contributes network access and computing resources, allowing the operator to distribute activity across many apparently unrelated systems.

Botnets support denial-of-service attacks, spam, credential abuse, malware delivery, and surveillance. The [[Mirai Botnet]] illustrates how weakly protected Internet-connected devices can turn a large population of ordinary products into attack infrastructure.

17634.content:
Bot Framework Emulator is a local client for connecting to a bot service during development. It displays the conversation, raw activity JSON, endpoint and network history, and can save a transcript for later inspection.

The bot remains an HTTP service even when the emulator makes it look like a chat window. Inspecting messages and network details helps separate dialog mistakes from endpoint, authentication, or serialization failures.

17637.heading: Bot Channel Registration
17637.content:
A bot channel registration connects a published bot endpoint to clients and communication channels managed through Azure. It names the bot, identifies the `/api/messages` endpoint, and supplies application credentials used by the deployed bot.

Registration is distinct from publishing the ASP.NET Core service: one makes the bot code reachable, while the other tells the channel infrastructure where and how to reach it. Configuration values can be stored as App Service settings instead of embedded in application files.

17640.heading: Bot Application Credentials
17640.content:
Bot application credentials consist of the Microsoft application identifier and secret associated with a bot channel registration. The Bot Framework uses them to authenticate communication involving the deployed bot.

The secret is shown only when created and must be recorded or regenerated. The project places these values in Azure App Service settings so deployment configuration can override empty development-file values without committing the secret to source.

17643.title: Bot Activity
17643.heading: Bot Activity
17643.content:
A bot activity is the structured message exchanged through Bot Framework. A message activity includes fields such as its sender, text, and activity type and is transported as JSON between a client, channel, and bot service.

The bot's activity handler receives the current turn and sends a reply activity through the turn context. A Direct Line client constructs the same kind of object when posting a user's message to an active conversation.

17646.title: Boredom in Games
17646.heading: Boredom in Games
17646.content:
Boredom in games can occur when the player's mastery exceeds the demands of the activity and the system asks only for repetition of already understood actions. Resistance remains, but it no longer produces significant learning or choice.

Avoiding boredom does not require constant escalation. New relationships, altered pacing, wider choices, or a deliberate reflective pause can change the experience without simply increasing [[Game Difficulty|difficulty]].

17649.title: Bootstrap Aggregating
17649.heading: Bootstrap Aggregating
17649.content:
Bootstrap aggregating, or bagging, trains base classifiers on samples drawn with replacement from the original training set and combines their outputs by voting or averaging. Resampling makes otherwise identical learners see different evidence.

Bagging is most effective for unstable algorithms whose fitted boundaries change substantially under small data perturbations. Averaging reduces that variance when the resulting errors are not perfectly correlated.

17652.title: Boost uBLAS Distance Computation
17652.heading: Boost uBLAS Distance Computation
17652.content:
Boost uBLAS supplies vectors, symmetric matrices, matrix-vector products, and inner products used by covariance-aware clustering calculations. Mahalanobis distance can form a difference vector, apply its matrix transformation, and take the square root of the resulting inner product.

Using a tested linear-algebra interface makes the implementation clearer than manual nested indexing. Dimensions and aliasing options still require explicit checks because template compilation cannot infer the semantic compatibility of a runtime schema.

17655.title: Boolean Algebra
17655.heading: Boolean Algebra
17655.content:
Boolean algebra manipulates propositions using [[Logical Operators]] and equivalence laws. Identity, idempotent, commutative, associative, distributive, double-negation, excluded-middle, contradiction, and De Morgan laws permit a formula to be replaced by one with the same truth values.

These replacements can simplify both proofs and [[Electronic Circuits]], because logically equivalent formulas describe circuits with the same input-output behavior.

17658.title: Boosting Engine
17658.heading: Boosting Engine
17658.content:
A boosting engine is a [[Reinforcing Loop]] in which a source produces a resource and the player chooses between spending it on an immediate action or investing it to increase future resource flow.

The investment-versus-action trade-off creates long-term strategic decisions. Without sufficient [[Braking Engine|brakes]], the loop can run away, stall through deadlock, or converge on a dominant strategy that collapses the [[Play Space]].

17661.title: Boosted Tree Iteration
17661.heading: Boosted Tree Iteration
17661.content:
A boosted tree iteration adds another tree to an existing ensemble to correct its current residual or gradient error. The number of rounds controls model capacity together with learning rate and tree complexity.

Too few rounds underfit, while too many can overfit unless regularization and validation guide stopping.

17664.heading: Boost Unit Test Suite for ClusLib
17664.content:
ClusLib uses the Boost unit-test framework to organize suites and cases for individual source components. Tests exercise classes such as discrete and continuous attribute metadata before those components are relied upon by datasets and algorithms.

Component-level tests localize failures and make refactoring safer. Numerical tests should compare within meaningful tolerances and include invalid inputs so both calculations and diagnostic paths are verified.
